title: Docker & DevOps
description: Containers, Compose and the DevOps practices around them.
resumo: An image is the immutable package (code + runtime); a container is the image running.
Dockerfile: a small base with a fixed version (`eclipse-temurin:21-jre`), a non-root user, no secrets, dependencies before code.
Containers are ephemeral: database data goes in a volume.
`docker compose up` starts the app and its dependencies; containers find each other by service name (`db:5432`), never localhost.
Never `latest`: pin versions so you can trace and roll back.
DevOps: the team that builds the software also runs it, with an automated CI/CD pipeline.

subsections.subtitle: What Is Docker?
subsections.description: Packaging an application with everything it needs to run.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** "it works on my machine": the server has another Java version, a missing library or a different OS configuration, and the application fails only there.

**Concept:** a container packages the application with its runtime and libraries, and runs isolated on any machine that has Docker. Unlike a virtual machine, it shares the host's kernel, so it starts in seconds and uses far less memory. An image is the template; a container is a running instance of it; a registry (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry) stores and distributes images.

**How it works:** the same image runs on your laptop, in CI and in production, so the environment is the same everywhere.
examples.code:
Virtual machine:  app | libs | guest OS | hypervisor | host OS | hardware
Container:        app | libs |          container runtime | host OS | hardware

docker run --rm -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27      # downloads the image and starts it
# open http://localhost:8080 — the same nginx on any machine

docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
docker ps                                  # running containers
examples.interview_question: How does Docker ensure consistency between environments, and how is a container different from a virtual machine?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Treating a container like a server you maintain by hand: opening a shell, installing packages, editing files. The changes are lost when the container is recreated. Change the Dockerfile, rebuild, and run the new image.
examples.code:
# WRONG: fixing a running container by hand
docker exec -it api sh
apk add curl && vi /app/config.yml        # gone when the container is recreated

# RIGHT: change the Dockerfile (or the config), rebuild, redeploy
docker build -t api:1.0.1 .
docker run -d api:1.0.1

subsections.subtitle: Images and Containers
subsections.description: What you build, ship and run.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** it is easy to mix up the words: what exactly do you build, push to a registry and run?

**Concept:** an image is a read-only template made of layers; each Dockerfile instruction adds one. It is identified by `name:tag` (and an immutable digest). A container is an image plus a thin writable layer and a running process. Many containers can run from one image, and removing a container deletes its writable layer.

**How it works:** Dockerfile → `docker build` → image → `docker push` to a registry → `docker run` → container.
examples.code:
# Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY target/app.jar app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

docker build -t shop-api:1.4.0 .     # Dockerfile -> image
docker images                        # local images
docker run -d --name api shop-api:1.4.0   # image -> container
docker ps                            # running containers
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between an image and a container?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Using the `latest` tag. It moves: today's build and next month's use different bases, and you cannot tell which version is running or roll back to it. Pin versions.
examples.code:
# WRONG
FROM eclipse-temurin:latest
docker run shop-api:latest

# RIGHT: fixed versions you can trace and roll back to
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
docker run shop-api:1.4.0

subsections.subtitle: Docker Compose
subsections.description: Running the application and its dependencies with one command.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the application needs PostgreSQL and Redis locally. That is three long `docker run` commands, in the right order, typed differently by every developer.

**Concept:** a `compose.yaml` file describes the services, their configuration, networks and volumes. `docker compose up` starts everything, and the services reach each other by service name on a shared network.

**How it works:** commit the file with the project, so anyone can start the full environment with one command. `docker compose down` stops and removes the containers.
examples.code:
# compose.yaml
services:
  app:
    image: shop-api:1.4.0
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop
      SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST: cache
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: shop
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
  cache:
    image: redis:7

docker compose up -d       # start everything in the background
docker compose logs -f app
docker compose down
examples.interview_question: How does Docker Compose help with local development of a Spring Boot application?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Using `localhost` to reach another container. Inside a container, `localhost` is the container itself, so the connection is refused. Use the service name.
examples.code:
# WRONG: localhost is the app container itself -> Connection refused
SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop

# RIGHT: the service name is the host name on the Compose network
SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop

subsections.subtitle: DevOps
subsections.description: One team responsible for building and running the software.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** developers "throw code over the wall" to operations. Releases happen every few months, deploys are manual and painful, and when production breaks each side blames the other.

**Concept:** DevOps is a culture plus a set of practices: the people who build the software also share responsibility for running it. The practices include CI/CD, infrastructure as code, monitoring, small and frequent releases, and blameless postmortems. The DORA metrics measure the result.

**How it works:** work flows in a loop — plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor — and what you learn in production feeds the next plan.
examples.code:
Before DevOps                              With DevOps
- a release every 3 months                 - small changes, deployed daily
- manual deploy with a 40-step runbook     - an automated pipeline, same steps every time
- ops meets the app on go-live day         - the team that builds it also runs it
- outage: who is to blame?                 - outage: blameless postmortem, fix the process
examples.interview_question: How does a DevOps culture improve collaboration between teams?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Treating DevOps as a job title or a tool: creating a separate "DevOps team" that receives the code and deploys it. That is the same wall with a new name. The goal is shared responsibility, supported by automation.
examples.code:
WRONG: Dev team -> "DevOps team" -> production
       (the hand-off and the wall are still there)

RIGHT: one team owns the service end to end,
       with a shared platform (pipelines, clusters, templates) that makes it easy

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation: CI/CD has its own topic: **DevOps & Infra → CI/CD**. It covers continuous integration, delivery vs deployment, pipelines in GitHub Actions, quality gates, secrets and promotion between environments.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation: Kubernetes and `kubectl` have their own topic, right after this one: **DevOps & Infra → Kubernetes & kubectl**. It goes from the cluster and the first commands to troubleshooting, Helm and RBAC.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you recreate the database container and every record is gone. And the application cannot find the database container.

**Concept:** containers are ephemeral: whatever is written to a container's filesystem disappears when it is removed. Volumes managed by Docker keep data outside the container's life cycle, which is what a database needs. User-defined networks — Compose creates one automatically — let containers find each other by service name: the application connects to `db:5432`, not to localhost.

**How it works:** `depends_on` only orders the startup; with a `healthcheck` and `condition: service_healthy`, the application waits until the database accepts connections.
examples.code:
# compose.yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - pg-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
  app:
    image: shop-api:1.4.0
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/postgres
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy   # waits until the database is ready

volumes:
  pg-data:
examples.interview_question: How do you persist data from a database running in a container?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: `docker compose down -v`. The `-v` also deletes the named volumes, so the local database is gone. Plain `down` removes the containers and keeps the data.
examples.code:
# WRONG: also removes the volumes — the data is gone
docker compose down -v

# RIGHT: remove the containers, keep the data
docker compose down

subsections.subtitle: Essential Docker Commands
subsections.description: Building, running and debugging containers day to day.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a container does not start, or starts and stops right away. Where do you look?

**Concept:** `docker ps -a` shows every container with its status and exit code; `docker logs` shows what the application printed; `docker exec` runs a command (such as a shell) inside a running container; `docker inspect` shows the full configuration — environment variables, ports, volumes.

**How it works:** debug in that order: status and exit code, then logs, then inspect the configuration. Common causes: a port already in use, a missing environment variable, an application listening only on 127.0.0.1 inside the container.
examples.code:
docker build -t shop-api:1.0 .
docker run -d --name api -p 8080:8080 shop-api:1.0
docker ps -a                    # status and exit code
docker logs -f api              # follow the logs
docker exec -it api sh          # a shell inside the container
docker inspect api              # full configuration
docker image prune              # remove unused images
examples.interview_question: Which commands do you use to debug a container that will not start?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: An application that listens on `127.0.0.1` inside the container. The port is mapped, but connections from outside never reach it, because the container's localhost is not reachable from the host. Listen on all interfaces (`0.0.0.0`). Spring Boot does this by default; some dev servers do not.
examples.code:
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 web
curl localhost:3000              # connection reset
docker logs web                  # "Listening on 127.0.0.1:3000"

# RIGHT: listen on all interfaces inside the container
HOST=0.0.0.0 npm start

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** images of 800 MB that take minutes to build, run as root and carry a password in one of their layers.

**Concept:** use a small base image with a fixed version (`eclipse-temurin:21-jre`, never `latest`); order instructions from least to most frequently changed to reuse the layer cache; use `.dockerignore` to keep `target/` and `.git` out of the build; run as a non-root user; never put secrets in the image — every layer can be read. Multi-stage builds separate compiling from the final image.

**How it works:** each instruction is a cached layer. When one changes, every layer after it is rebuilt — that is why dependencies go before the source code.
examples.code:
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd --system app
COPY target/app.jar app.jar
USER app
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
examples.interview_question: Which practices make a Docker image smaller and more secure?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Copying all the source before downloading dependencies. Any code change invalidates the cache, so every build downloads all dependencies again. Copy the `pom.xml` and resolve dependencies first, then the code.
examples.code:
# WRONG: any code change re-downloads every dependency
COPY . .
RUN mvn -q package

# RIGHT: dependencies first (they change rarely), code last
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src src
RUN mvn -q -DskipTests package
